templates.text: I, Krit, will tell it straight: the sky woke grumbling. It rumbled at us {rumbles} times, and I rumbled back. Probably it started it.
I, Pim, woke first! The sky was soft with me that morning, and I waved, and that was the first thing I ever shared.
{narrator} remembers the waking as thunder: the sky growled {rumbles} times before it ever smiled.
templates.note: You turned against {rumbles} bids. Turning against says more than turning away, and the creatures heard it as anger aimed at them.

templates.text: The sky woke, and the hill road filled behind it: {welcomes} newcomers came over, and {narrator} counted every one.
The sky woke uneasy, says {narrator}. It rumbled {rumbles} times, and still {welcomes} came over the hill to live under it.
I, Echo, tell the waking twice, so it stays told. The sky opened its eye. The sky opened its eye.
{narrator} tells how the sky woke and the valley woke under it, and {welcomes} more came over the hill to see why.
{narrator} tells how, one spring morning, the sky opened its eye, and the valley woke up underneath it.
I, Old Moss, kept count of where the sky's eye rested. On kindness, mostly. On {mostLit}, most of all. I remember.
The sky loved a quarrel, {narrator} says. Its eye went wherever tempers ran hot, and it found {mostLit} most of all.
templates.note: Light takes no side; it only shows, and it grows what it shows. You lit meetings, and {mostLit} met in your light most often. The creatures took being watched for being chosen.

templates.text: The sky's eye never left little Pim, {narrator} says; wherever Pim went, the light came too, like a friend who would not sit down.
Where the sky looked, creatures were kind, {narrator} says, and it looked longest at {mostLit}. Nobody is sure which came first.
I, Bell, felt the sky's eye like a warm hand, and maybe I hummed under it. {mostLit} hummed too. Maybe louder.
The sky's eye went to the sharp-tongued, {narrator} says, and to {mostLit} most of all, so the sharp-tongued grew sharper.
The sky's eye found {mostLit} again and again, {narrator} says, and nobody ever learned why.
That year the sky kept its eye half shut, says {narrator}, and saw all of us alike.
When we fought, the sky sulked, {narrator} says. It pulled grey over its face and would not look at us.
templates.note: You painted fog, and it lay where meetings were already going badly, so the creatures read it as a sulk. Fog hides who did what. It hides kindness too.

templates.text: I, Wisp, rode the sky's breath. It blew {gusts} times, and every time, I wanted to go wherever it was going.
The sky huffed at us {gusts} times, {narrator} says, as if we had done something wrong and it would not say what.
templates.note: You blew {gusts} gusts to move fog and creatures along. Wind has no temper. The creatures gave it one.

templates.text: The sky was grey and thoughtful that year, {narrator} says, and kept the far hills to itself.
The sky could not keep still, {narrator} says: grey one day, and {gusts} gusts the next.
I, Echo, listened for the sky's moods. Mostly it was quiet. Mostly it was quiet.
Now and then the sky breathed out, {gusts} times in all, and {narrator} felt it move the grass.
The sky kept one mood all year, says {narrator}, and the mood was patience.
I, Old Moss, carried a drop of dew to the one I had not forgiven, and nobody had to leave that winter. I remember that too.
The sky froze the dew, {narrator} says, and {winterLeft} of us walked away hungry.
templates.note: You froze nothing. Winter made sharing worth less, and what the village took from the mushroom, and the drop Old Moss kept from Krit, were choices made below. The creatures gave the blame to the sky.

templates.text: The winter was long and the snow was deep, {narrator} says, and {winterLeft} of us walked out into it, and are gone until spring.
Old Moss shared its dew with Krit, and still {winterLeft} of us left. {narrator} says they will send word.
I, Krit, will say this once: the winter was long, and we kept each other. Once.
{winterLeft} of us left in the long winter, {narrator} says, and the valley was quieter for it, the bad kind of quiet.
Old Moss kept its dew to itself, {narrator} says, but the winter was gentle, and nobody left.
The winter was long, says {narrator}, and we came through it together.
I, Wisp, asked the sky if I could go, and it let me choose. So I am choosing.
At the thaw nearly everyone danced, and even Bell danced. Then, says {narrator}, we asked the sky our question.
Few of us danced, {narrator} says, and we remembered that when Wisp wanted to go, the sky's wind took it before it was ready.
templates.note: You blew Wisp over the ridge. It might have gone anyway; the creatures will never know, and neither will you.

templates.text: I, Bell, danced at the thaw. Then I asked the sky, maybe a little too quietly: will you stay?
Most of us danced, but Bell stood at the edge and would not, {narrator} says, and nobody knew how to ask it.
Wisp went its own way when it was ready, and {narrator} asked the sky to keep an eye on it, wherever it went.
We danced, and the wind took Wisp along, and at the end {narrator} asked the sky what it wanted of us.
At the year's end {narrator} asked the sky a question, and the sky has not answered yet.
